hh_hamilton_richard_j.note: MOVED OFF THE AGENCY HOUSE AND ONTO HIS OWN, 2026-09-27 UNDER T-1625, AND THE GRADE DID NOT MOVE WITH IT. The note this replaces said the link to `cobweb_castle` rested on one sentence of Andreas — 'In the fall of 1832, Colonel Hamilton and Colonel Owen employed John Watkins to teach a small school in the North Division, near the old Indian agency-house in which Colonel Hamilton then resided' — nearly three years before 1 July 1835, and it said in as many words that 'nothing reached follows him out of it or keeps him in it'. SOMETHING NOW FOLLOWS HIM OUT OF IT. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago vol. 2 p. 155, read as `bk_mose2_006`, give the whole sequence: he 'lived first in the fort and, when that grew too crowded with the refugees, he moved to the Agency House; and in 1833, with Col. Owen, hired John Watkins to teach the little school in the old stable near by. At about this time he built his house on what is now Michigan street between Cass and Rush, where he lived for nineteen years.' The first two stages corroborate Andreas — the fort, then the Agency House, then the same two colonels hiring the same schoolmaster in the same year — and the third stage is the one Andreas does not have: a house of his own, built about 1833, held for nineteen years. Nineteen years from 1833 runs to about 1852 and 1835-07-01 falls inside it, so this is a SPAN enclosing the scene date rather than a fact dated outside it and carried back. THE STRUCTURE IT NAMES IS AN IDENTIFICATION AND NOT A STATEMENT. `watkins_school_house` is this project's record of the house on Michigan Street between Cass and Rush that Andreas has Watkins teaching in 'later'; Andreas names no owner for it and Moses and Kirkland name no school in Hamilton's. The join is Hamilton himself, who hired the schoolmaster, and the reasoning, the caveat that no source gives the SIDE of Michigan Street Hamilton built on, and what would refute the whole thing are written on that record's `occupants` block rather than repeated here. NOTHING IS PROMOTED. Moses and Kirkland is a compilation of 1895; under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 it corroborates and dates and may not raise a confidence, so this stays `inferred` exactly as it was when it pointed at the Agency House. What changed is that the inference now runs forward from a span that covers the scene date instead of backward from a sentence about 1832. The record names a committed structure; the roof is the evidence's own limit and nothing narrower is claimed. COPIED FROM THE SINGULAR `lives_at` AND ITS RECONCILIATION ROW `hh_hamilton_richard_j#lives_at`, changing no value, confidence or source. That field names the place as of 1 July 1835 and dates neither end of the relationship, so this row is `undated` rather than borrowing the scene date as a start (T-1273)

hh_kimberly_edmund_s.note: SEATED BY T-2140 IN THE HOUSE BONNELL GIVES HIM. J. D. Bonnell's letter of 1876, quoted by Andreas (vol. 1, printed pages 136-137): "east of which [the Lake House] was the residence of Dr. Kimball, who was a partner of Mr. Pruyne in a drug store on South Water Street." A doctor, Pruyne's partner, and a druggist on South Water Street identify this man three ways over; data/structures/kimberly_residence.json raised the building on that sentence and named him its occupant, and refused to write the household link while he shared a record with Pruyne, because seating the partnership there would have carried Pruyne across the river on a sentence about Kimberly. With the two men on two records the link is written from this side, which is the direction the evidence runs in. GRADED AT THE INFERENCE, NOT THE SENTENCE: the walk is the morning of 26 August 1835, eight weeks after the scene date, and the carry back to 1 July is the inference. A LATER DIRECTORY AGREES AND IS NOT LEANED ON: Fergus's 1839 directory prints 'Kimberly, Dr. Edmund S., res. N. Water st next Lake House' (f1839_e0850) - the same spot four years on, which corroborates the house and dates nothing in 1835. The record names a committed structure; the roof is the evidence's own limit and nothing narrower is claimed. hh_rc_cavanagh_edward.note: SEATED AT THE BARRACKS, AND T-1715 RE-EXAMINED THAT AGAINST THE PLAN THE CARD ASKS FOR. The 1835 General Regulations quarter washerwomen inside the same allowance as the men (art. 31), so the barracks is where the Regulations themselves put them and the seating is not a shortcut. The plan this project holds is the 1830 Harrison survey, and it was read again for this: it letters the barn, the wash house, the shop, the well and a pair of blocks it calls `Out Buildings`, and it letters NO married quarters. The pair is the only candidate and it is refused — 24 x 19 ft and 13 x 10 ft, unlabelled, and already built as `fort_dearborn_out_building_a` and `_b` on a record that declines to name a use; moving eight households onto them would be naming one. A hut outside the palisade, which is where married soldiers often were, is still a structure nobody drew. WHAT CHANGED IS THE ARITHMETIC THAT ARGUED AGAINST IT: the quartering check used to report the barracks 26 quarters short and offer the storey count as an open reading, and the record asserts two storeys, so on what stands the allowance is met with room over. The seating is still reconstructed and still replaceable by a plan that assigns quarters; it is no longer the weakest line on this card. Reconstructed on the rule `no_married_quarters_are_drawn_so_the_barracks_carries_them`; no source places this household.
